# Periodic Trends

## Core ideas and reasoning

A trend needs an explanation from charge, distance and shielding. Across a period proton number increases while added electrons enter the same main shell. Increasing effective nuclear attraction generally decreases atomic radius and raises the energy needed to remove an outer electron, with exceptions due to subshell arrangements. Down a main group more occupied shells increase distance and shielding, so atomic radius generally increases. Group I metals become more reactive down the group because the outer electron is lost more readily. Halogens become less reactive down the group as attraction for an added electron becomes less effective. Compare ions with their parent atoms carefully: a positive ion is usually smaller and a negative ion larger. For isoelectronic ions with the same electron count, greater nuclear charge generally gives the smaller radius. Do not explain a trend simply by saying reactivity increases; identify the electron transfer and the physical reason for it.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Explain why atomic radius generally decreases from sodium to chlorine across Period 3.

Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main shell. Greater effective attraction pulls the electron cloud closer, so radius decreases.

### Example 2

Why is potassium more reactive than sodium in typical Group I reactions?

Potassium’s outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is more easily lost.

### Example 3

Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ each have 10 electrons. Which is smaller and why?

Mg²⁺ is smaller because its 12 protons attract the same number of electrons more strongly than sodium’s 11 protons.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
